episodes.171308: A strong thunderstorm became severe around 1800 LST on the east side of Huntsville atop Monte Sano Mountain.  A young hiker was killed when a tree limb hit him on the head while hiking Bluff Line Trail of Monte Sano Nature Preserve.  At the nearby Monte Sano Campground, at least one large tree and numerous large tree limbs were knocked down.  A number of awnings of motor homes/campers were damage as well.
episodes.171309: Monsoon moisture increased across western Colorado as a shortwave trough undercut a ridge of high pressure over the Great Basin. This led to increased shower and thunderstorm activity across the Western Slope. Storms were slow moving and produced heavy rain. Localized debris flows occurred in Gunnison and Mesa counties.
episodes.171319: An easterly wave that had been impacting southern New Mexico all week was now located over southern Arizona on August 19, 2022. Continued moisture advection into western and southern New Mexico generated widespread showers and thunderstorms across the area by late morning on the 19th. A thunderstorm over the McBride burn scar produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding and debris flow.
episodes.171390: The combination of deep moisture, modest mixed-layer convective available potential energy and forcing associated with shortwave energy aloft and a nearly stationary front led to conditions favorable for heavy rainfall and localized flash flooding.
episodes.171391: A warm and unstable airmass positioned under a right entrance region of an upper level jet along with a nearby trough of low pressure and late afternoon sea breeze circulation led to severe thunderstorms with hail and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.171392: A warm and unstable airmass positioned under a right entrance region of an upper level jet along with a nearby trough of low pressure and late afternoon sea breeze circulation led to severe thunderstorms with hail and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.171728: A thunderstorm outflow wind knocked down several large trees and power lines outside of McCall. The McCall airport recorded a gust of 45 mph.
episodes.171991: A cold front brought isolated to scattered severe thunderstorms with large hail to portions of South Central Nebraska on the evening of August 18th. The first signs of thunderstorm development along the cold front showed itself in Valley County between 3 PM to 4 PM CDT. Temperatures ahead of the front were in the 80s, which was supportive of moderate instability. As instability increased ahead of the front between 4 PM and 5 PM, thunderstorms strengthened and became severe on an isolated basis roughly near the Highway 92 corridor. By 5 PM, a storm near Ravenna in far northeast Buffalo County developed supercell characteristics and began to produce significant amounts of large hail, including up to golf ball size. This storm weakened as it moved southeast through eastern Buffalo County by 6 PM, but a new intense storm developed over central Buffalo County and also became severe and produced large hail just northeast and east of Kearney in the Gibbon area. Around the same time, a lone/isolated supercell developed just north of Genoa along the Boone/Platte County line and quickly became severe. This storm slowly moved south into eastern Nance County between 6:00-6:30 PM, and ended up producing the largest hail of the evening, up to baseball size, in and around Genoa. Significant damage occurred as a result, particularly to crops, vehicles, and roofs. The storm weakened as it moved into Polk County, but still managed to produce severe hail up to ping pong ball size in western Polk County between 7-7:30 PM. Activity quickly decreased in coverage and severity as nocturnal cooling set in between 7:30-8 PM.
episodes.171992: The vast majority of regional severe weather on this Thursday afternoon-evening focused slightly to the north of the local area (within south central Nebraska) between 4:30-7:30 PM CDT. However, as a cold front moved into North Central Kansas during the late evening, a single storm managed to pulse back up to severe levels in far western Phillips County between 8:30-9 PM. The lone severe report with this storm was quarter size hail in Prairie View. This storm weakened as it moved south into Rooks County during the late evening hours.
episodes.172302: A week cold front initiated storms in eastern Nebraska resulting in widespread hail reports with the largest size reported at 2.75.
episodes.172303: A stalled/slowly moving cold front initiated storms in southeast Nebraska leading to a few hail and wind reports.
episodes.172384: Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along the mountain ridges on the afternoon of August 19th. Strong winds that accompanied these storms resulted in single tree damage both in the towns of War and Welch in McDowell County.
episodes.172424: Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of August 19th in southwest Virginia. Locally heavy rainfall resulted in one instance of high water issues along Dante Mountain Road in Dickenson County through the early evening hours.
episodes.172518: A frontal boundary across southern Georgia slowly lifted northward resulting in moist southwest steering flow over the area. Storms along the West Coast sea breeze pushed inland and interacted with the East Coast sea breeze in the late afternoon. Moist airmass (PWATs > 2 in.), ample instability and sea breeze boundary collision led to a severe storm developing in Flagler county. This storm knocked down trees which damaged utility equipment in Daytona North.
episodes.172593: Strong thunderstorms produced a funnel cloud and flash flooding.
episodes.173094: A few storms over north central Kansas produced very localized severe weather in Lincoln County.  Another rogue storm in south central Kansas produced a severe wind gust also.
episodes.173303: Scattered storms moved across portions of northeast Iowa during the late afternoon of August 19th. These storms dropped some hail, the largest reported being quarter sized in Oelwein (Fayette County).
episodes.173330: An upper trough pulled up stationary across Northeast Texas, extreme Southern Arkansas and North Louisiana during the morning of August 18th, which reinforced a weak surface front south into Deep East Texas and Central Louisiana. This front focused an area of low level moisture pooling across these areas, as well as increased large scale forcing as it tapped into strong heating during the afternoon. Weak steering currents were noted aloft, resulting in an area of slow moving thunderstorms developing across Southern Cherokee and much of Angelina Counties in Deep East Texas, with widespread rainfall amounts of two to four inches falling across these areas in a short period of time. Thus, flash flooding was observed in Downtown Lufkin in Angelina County where a couple of roads were covered in high water.
episodes.173446: A cold core low moved over the area, dragging along a weak and slow moving surface low. Although weak, sufficient low level and upper forcing aided in developing strong to severe storms. Instability and shear were strong enough for a few supercell thunderstorms to develop and bring hail, strong winds, and heavy rain to the area. The storms were slow moving. which allowed some storms to anchor over locations for an extended period of time, resulting in flash flooding. Some repeated storms over the same area also led to similar results. Severe weather reports were mostly in the form of hail, as these storms produced hail very efficiently. The largest hail reported was 1.5, and there were some isolated reports of damaging winds.
episodes.173503: A surface low sinking south into the area allowed for scattered storms to develop across central Iowa in the afternoon. Steep lapse rates and deep layer shear allowed for the development of organized updrafts while low melting levels supported larger hail development. Several storms strengthened and prompted warnings, though few resulted in any severe reports. The strongest quickly developed over the Des Moines metro, where the time between a clear radar image and golf ball sized hail was just over 20 minutes. Hail pummeled the west side of the metro for nearly 30 minutes, resulting in hundreds of vehicles with significant damage. One high school in West Des Moines also reported damage to the building which resulted in water leaking into the library and a rush to protect the books. After the hail ended the storms continued to train across the metro, resulting in flash flooding a a couple of water rescues due to stranded vehicles.
episodes.173660: Thunderstorms moved northwest across southeast Arizona during the afternoon. Heavy rain resulted in flash flooding in parts of the Tucson Metro area and a funnel cloud was spotted near Three Points.
episodes.173689: Favorable monsoonal conditions promoted the development of severe thunderstorms across the region on the 18th. Abundant moisture (PWATs of 1.7-2.0) and instability (MUCAPE 1,000-2,000 J/kg) was in place across south-central and southwest Arizona, while increased easterly steering flow from an upper level low over northern Mexico aided in thunderstorms propagating off the high terrain. DCAPE were around 1,000-1,200 J/kg which helped in allowing strong to severe thunderstorms to produce damaging winds from downbursts. Thunderstorms initially developed along the Mogollon Rim during the early afternoon hours before pushing into the lower deserts of south-central and southwest Arizona through the evening. No injuries were reported.
episodes.173693: Thunderstorms over the higher terrain of northern Arizona pushed southwest into the lower deserts during the evening of the 18th. These thunderstorms continued in a favorable environment characterized by abundant moisture (PWATs around 1.8-1.9) and high instability (MUCAPE around 2,000 J/kg). As these thunderstorms moved through the Lower Colorado River Valley area near Blythe, they produced damaging winds and flash flooding. No injuries were reported.
episodes.173705: Thunderstorms on the 19th initiated across southeast Arizona and along the Mogollon Rim during the late morning/early afternoon hours before pushing into the lower elevations of south-central Arizona. A couple of upper level features, which included an area of low pressure over northern Sonora and a shortwave trough over the Great Basin, aided in ascent over the region in an environment characterized by high instability (MUCAPE 2,000 J/kg) and anomalously high moisture (PWATs 1.8-2.2). Given the moisture in place, thunderstorms were able to become efficient rainfall producers, leading to multiple reports of flash flooding across the area. No injuries were reported.
episodes.173733: Thunderstorms resulted in flash flooding over several days, which included Zion National Park.
episodes.173800: Persistent moist monsoonal flow fueled thunderstorms over southeast California. Several storms produced flash flooding, and a few produced severe weather.
episodes.173801: Persistent moist monsoonal flow fueled thunderstorms over northwest Arizona. Several storms produced flash flooding.
episodes.173802: Persistent moist monsoonal flow fueled spotty thunderstorms over southern Nevada. One storm produced wind damage.
episodes.173839: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening hours on August 19. A few storms were nearly stationary and dumped very heavy rainfall in a short amount of time. One such storm occurred in far northeastern Rutherford County with some flooding reported.
episodes.173880: A cold front plowed into an environment with roughly 1500 J/kg MLCAPE but weak shear, which resulted in numerous thunderstorms with brief intense updrafts. The strongest storms produced isolated damaging wind gusts and hail up to golf ball size. By evening, a stronger low-level flow ahead of the front resulted in a slightly stronger storm with hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter across northwest Iowa.
episodes.173986: Deep monsoon moisture over northern Arizona brought strong thunderstorms and local flash flooding.

Flows increased on the North Fork of the Virgin River in Zion National Park. The trail became impassable near the mouth of The Narrows. Flood waters in The Narrows swept some hikers off their feet and isolated others on higher ground. Two people were swept downstream. One was swept a couple of hundred yards and found. The individual survived with minor injuries. The other was reported as missing to Zion National Park officials later that evening, and was found deceased the following Monday. The North Fork Virgin - Springdale river gauge, which is downstream from The Narrows, rose from approximately 75 cfs to 735 cfs, corresponding to a rise of slightly over 2 feet in height.
